questions.q: A 3-day-old Black neonate presents with a poorly circumscribed, grayish-blue macular patch measuring 8 cm over the lumbosacral region. The parents ask why the lesion appears blue rather than brown. Which optical phenomenon best explains this clinical presentation?
opts: Rayleigh scattering of longer wavelengths by superficial epidermal melanin
Tyndall effect causing shorter blue wavelengths to scatter back from deep dermal melanin
Mie scattering from collagen bundles in the papillary dermis
Selective absorption of red light by dermal hemoglobin
questions.exp: The characteristic bluish-gray hue of Mongolian spots results from the Tyndall effect, wherein shorter blue light wavelengths are preferentially scattered back to the observer's eye by melanin granules located in the deep reticular dermis. This is an optical illusion rather than a true change in melanin color. The deeper location of melanocytes (compared to epidermal melanin) creates this distinctive clinical appearance.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with multiple dark brown macules on his trunk, widely spaced eyes, and a cardiac murmur consistent with pulmonary stenosis. He has sensorineural hearing loss and short stature. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Cardio-facio-cutaneous syndrome (CFCS)
LEOPARD syndrome
Costello syndrome
Noonan syndrome
questions.exp: LEOPARD syndrome is defined by the classic acronym: Lentigines, ECG abnormalities, Ocular hypertelorism, Pulmonary stenosis, Abnormalities of genitalia, Retardation of growth, and Deafness. This patient presents with multiple features matching this mnemonic exactly. All RASopathies share Ras/MAPK pathway mutations but have distinct syndromic presentations.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: A LEOPARD wearing spotted DOTS (Lentigines) spots a WIDE-EYED OWL (Ocular hypertelorism) in the PULMONARY tower, while DEAF GUARDS (Deafness) miss SHORT soldiers (Retardation of growth) marching past the CARDIAC gate—remember L-E-O-P-A-R-D in the throne room!

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with a rapidly growing, firm, dome-shaped papule on his neck that is pink-red in color and measures 5 mm. Histology shows symmetrical, well-circumscribed architecture with large plump epithelioid and spindle melanocytes displaying abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Which pathognomonic histological finding would most strongly support a diagnosis of classic Spitz nevus?
opts: Junctional activity with individual cell maturation at the basal layer
Kamino bodies—dull-pink, acellular, eosinophilic globules of basement membrane material that are PAS-positive
Mitotic figures predominantly in the superficial dermis with loss of maturation with depth
Heavily pigmented nests confined exclusively to the epidermis with a starburst dermoscopic pattern
questions.exp: Kamino bodies are pathognomonic eosinophilic, PAS-positive globules of basement membrane material found within the epidermis and at the dermal-epidermal junction in classic Spitz nevi. They are a critical diagnostic feature that distinguishes Spitz nevi from melanoma and other melanocytic lesions. Maturation with depth (progressive cell size reduction into the deeper dermis) is also a hallmark of benign classic Spitz nevi.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture KAMINO (the Fire Nation capital) burning with PINK FIRE inside the castle's basement (DEJ)—that's your PAS-positive basement membrane goo marking the Spitz throne room.

questions.q: Xeroderma pigmentosum is fundamentally distinct from autoimmune blistering disorders because its pathogenesis involves defective repair of which specific ultraviolet radiation-induced DNA photoproducts?
opts: Thymine-adenine transversions and guanine-cytosine mutations
Cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and pyrimidine (6-4) pyrimidone photoproducts
Histone acetylation marks and chromatin remodeling complexes
Oxidative stress-induced 8-oxoguanine lesions only
questions.exp: XP is a disorder of genomic instability caused by mutations in DNA repair enzymes that normally repair cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPDs) and pyrimidine (6-4) pyrimidone photoproducts induced by ultraviolet radiation. Unlike autoimmune diseases, XP has no pathogenic antibodies, target autoantigens, or HLA associations; instead, the defect lies in nuclear DNA repair enzymes critical for maintaining genomic integrity.

questions.q: A 6-month-old infant of Asian descent is found to have extensive, dark Mongolian spots involving the trunk, shoulders, extremities, and ventral chest—far exceeding the typical lumbosacral distribution. Which metabolic screening should be prioritized to rule out a serious underlying condition?
opts: Thyroid function tests and anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies
Lysosomal enzyme panel and urine glycosaminoglycans to exclude storage diseases such as GM1 gangliosidosis, Hurler's disease, or Hunter's disease
HLA typing and serum immunoglobulin levels
Serum glucose and 24-hour urinary catecholamines
questions.exp: Extensive, dark, and progressive Mongolian spots that extend beyond the classic sacral region are a major cutaneous red flag for underlying inborn errors of metabolism, particularly lysosomal storage diseases including GM1 gangliosidosis type 1, Hurler's disease (MPS I), Hunter's disease (MPS II), Niemann-Pick disease, mannosidosis, and mucolipidosis II. Evaluation with lysosomal enzyme assays and urine glycosaminoglycans is essential in these atypical presentations.

questions.q: A 10-month-old infant presents with a 4-day history of high fever (104.5°F) and appears otherwise well. On day 5, as the fever subsides, a rose-pink maculopapular rash with white halos appears on the trunk and neck. Which cellular receptor does the causative HHV-6B virus utilize for cellular entry?
opts: CD4 receptor on T-lymphocytes
CD46 immune regulatory protein
Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)
Intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1)
questions.exp: HHV-6B, the primary cause of classic roseola infantum, utilizes CD46 as its cellular receptor for entry. In contrast, HHV-7 uses the CD4 receptor on T-lymphocytes. Both viruses primarily target CD4+ T lymphocytes for active infection but can also infect monocytes, NK cells, epithelial cells, and neuronal cells.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture HHV-6B knocking on a DOOR (CD46) at the castle gate while HHV-7 uses the CD4 ROYAL CARPET ENTRANCE—two different keys, same T-cell mansion.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child with a family history of atopic dermatitis and asthma develops frictional lichenoid eruption. On histology, which finding would you expect to see?
opts: Band-like lichenoid interface dermatitis with basal layer destruction
Mild spongiotic dermatitis with hyperkeratosis and superficial perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate
Subcorneal acantholysis with pemphigus-like changes
Dermal fibrosis with sclerotic collagen deposition
questions.exp: Despite the name 'lichenoid,' frictional lichenoid eruption shows a non-specific mild subacute spongiotic dermatitis rather than true lichenoid interface dermatitis. Histology reveals intercellular edema (spongiosis), hyperkeratosis, focal parakeratosis, and mild superficial perivascular inflammation—features consistent with an atopic eczematous response to friction.

questions.q: A geneticist explains to parents that their infant's cardiac and cutaneous abnormalities are caused by de novo mutations affecting intracellular signaling, not by autoimmune mechanisms. Which intracellular pathway is the primary molecular target in cardio-facio-cutaneous spectrum disorders?
opts: Complement and HLA-mediated immune complex deposition
Ras/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling cascade
T-cell receptor (TCR) antigen recognition
Interleukin-6 inflammatory cytokine pathway
questions.exp: Cardio-facio-cutaneous spectrum disorders (RASopathies) are caused by de novo germ-line mutations that aberrantly activate the Ras/MAPK intracellular signaling cascade. Unlike autoimmune conditions, they lack specific target autoantigens, pathogenic antibodies, or HLA associations. The diagnosis depends on recognizing the syndromic constellation of findings rather than serology.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: Inside the castle's SIGNAL TOWER, a RAS KNIGHT activates the MAPK ARMY (not immune soldiers!), launching arrows at developmental targets—draw a giant blue RAS-MAPK PIPELINE across the throne room to remember it's purely genetic signaling, NO ANTIBODIES allowed!

questions.q: A 9-year-old girl develops a painful, deep, solitary plantar wart on her heel that has been present for 3 months and is highly resistant to treatment. Histology shows prominent, large eosinophilic keratohyalin inclusion granules and marked endophytic growth. Which specific HPV type and wart subtype combination best explains these findings?
opts: HPV-2, mosaic warts
HPV-1, myrmecia
HPV-3, flat warts
HPV-4, palmar warts
questions.exp: Myrmecia is a specific, highly painful variant of deep plantar warts caused almost exclusively by HPV-1. These warts are characterized by endophytic growth with prominent, large eosinophilic keratohyalin inclusion granules in the cytoplasm. Mosaic warts (HPV-2) are multiple superficial lesions forming a pavement-like plaque, not a solitary deep wart. Flat and palmar warts have different HPV associations and histological features.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine MYRMECIA (ant colony) with giant ANTS digging DEEP into the HEEL CHAMBER—each ant carries a HUGE YELLOW CRYSTAL (keratohyalin granule), and only HPV-1 ants build these elaborate underground fortresses.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with multiple dome-shaped, flesh-colored papules on his hands with pathognomonic black dots on the surface. Histological examination reveals hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, papillomatosis with 'church spire' formations, and vacuolated keratinocytes with pyknotic nuclei surrounded by clear perinuclear halos in the upper stratum spinosum. Which HPV type is most likely responsible?
opts: HPV-3
HPV-1
HPV-10
HPV-28
questions.exp: Common warts (verruca vulgaris) are caused by HPV 1, 2, 4, 27, and 57. The black dots represent thrombosed capillary loops, and the pathognomonic histological finding is koilocytes (vacuolated keratinocytes with shrunken, hyperchromatic nuclei and perinuclear halos) in the upper stratum spinosum and granulosum with characteristic 'church spire' papillomatosis. HPV-3, 10, and 28 cause flat warts, not common warts.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a CHURCH made of SPIRES in the castle—inside, KOILOCYTES wearing HALOS (like monks) sit at the TOP FLOOR, proving they're COMMON WARTS with HPV-1,2,4,27,57 attending services.

questions.q: Electron microscopy in a neonate with severe congenital ichthyosis reveals abnormal, empty, or entirely missing lamellar bodies in the stratum granulosum, along with absence of extracellular lipid lamellae. What is the primary consequence of this ultrastructural pathology?
opts: Impaired melanin distribution leading to hyperpigmentation
Massive breakdown of the skin's permeability barrier with failure to establish intercellular lipid scaffolding
Excessive keratinocyte proliferation in the basal layer triggering hyperplasia
Abnormal collagen synthesis in the dermal-epidermal junction
questions.exp: The absence of lamellar bodies and extracellular lipid lamellae in Harlequin ichthyosis (ABCA12-mutated classic type) results in failure to form the critical intercellular lipid bilayers of the stratum corneum. This causes a catastrophic breakdown of the permeability barrier, rendering the neonate susceptible to massive transepidermal water loss, hypernatremic dehydration, temperature instability, and life-threatening complications.
questions.memory_palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine the castle's BRICK WALL (stratum corneum) is built with EMPTY CRATES (missing lamellar bodies) and INVISIBLE MORTAR (absent lipid lamellae). The wall CRUMBLES instantly—water floods in, salt crystals accumulate, the fortress becomes a desiccated ruin. No lipid scaffold = FORTRESS FAILURE.

questions.q: Regarding the pathogenesis of Kawasaki Disease, which of the following statements is CORRECT?
opts: The disease is driven by host autoantibodies against specific coronary artery adhesion molecules, similar to pemphigus vulgaris
A specific causative agent has been cultured in conventional media from affected patients, confirming bacterial etiology

Kawasaki Disease is a systemic vasculitis of medium-sized muscular arteries triggered by an unidentified ubiquitous infectious agent in a genetically susceptible host, with vascular damage occurring via neutrophilic necrotizing arteritis, CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-driven vasculitis, and luminal myofibroblastic proliferation
The disease exclusively affects the cutaneous microvasculature, with coronary involvement occurring only in untreated cases after 12 weeks of illness
questions.exp: Kawasaki Disease lacks a known host autoantigen and is NOT a classic autoimmune disease like pemphigus. Cultures are sterile, and the exact causative agent remains unknown. The pathogenesis involves three linked mechanisms: (1) neutrophilic necrotizing arteritis in the first 2 weeks destroying the internal elastic lamina, (2) subacute/chronic CD8+ T-lymphocyte and IgA plasma cell-driven vasculitis, and (3) luminal myofibroblastic proliferation leading to stenosis and thrombosis.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with severe blistering sunburns after minimal sun exposure, progressive neurological decline, growth retardation, and hypogonadism. Genetic testing reveals mutations in the XPA gene. Which of the following best describes the primary defect in his DNA repair pathway?
opts: Defective helicase activity in the TFIIH transcription/repair complex
Impaired DNA damage verification in the nucleotide excision repair pathway
Loss of translesion synthesis polymerase function
Defective mismatch repair enzyme complex
questions.exp: XP-A results from mutations in the XPA gene encoding the XPA protein, which is responsible for DNA damage verification in the NER pathway. The severe neurological phenotype with mental deficiency, dwarfism, and gonadal hypoplasia defines De Sanctis-Cacchione Syndrome, which occurs with complete loss-of-function XPA mutations. XP-B involves ERCC3/XPB helicase defects, while XP-Variant involves translesion synthesis defects.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with sudden onset of a single round patch of complete hair loss on the scalp. Dermoscopy reveals short hairs that are narrower at the proximal end and wider distally. Which of the following best explains why this child retains the potential for complete hair regrowth despite years of hair loss?
opts: The hair bulge region containing follicular stem cells is spared from autoimmune attack
Melanocyte-associated antigens are the only targets of the immune system
The inflammatory infiltrate is composed exclusively of CD4+ T-cells
HLA-DQB1*03 mutations spontaneously reverse with time
questions.exp: Alopecia areata is a non-cicatricial (non-scarring) alopecia because the autoimmune attack is strictly localized to the peribulbar region of the anagen hair follicle, while the bulge region (upper follicular stem cell reservoir) is spared. This preservation of stem cells explains the potential for complete regrowth. The narrower hairs with wider distal ends are exclamation mark hairs characteristic of active patches.
questions.source: [paeds Day 28] Alopecia areata in children + JAKi
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture the hair bulge as a FORTIFIED BULGE TOWER at the top of a castle—the immune knights only attack the LOWER BULB DUNGEON, leaving the tower's STEM CELL GUARDS untouched and ready to rebuild everything from scratch.

questions.q: A 10-month-old infant presents with high fever for 6 days, bilateral conjunctival injection, and a polymorphous rash. On examination, cervical lymphadenopathy and strawberry tongue are noted, but oral mucosal changes are absent. Echocardiography reveals coronary artery dilation. Which classification of Kawasaki Disease does this case represent, and why is early recognition critical in this age group?
opts: Classic Kawasaki Disease; infants have better prognosis with delayed treatment
Incomplete Kawasaki Disease; infants <6 months are paradoxically at highest risk for severe coronary complications due to delayed diagnosis
Incomplete Kawasaki Disease; adult presentation is more common in immunocompromised hosts
Adult-onset Kawasaki Disease; presentation in infancy carries negligible coronary risk
questions.exp: Incomplete Kawasaki Disease is defined by fever ≥5 days with only 2–3 classic features (this case lacks one criterion), and it is most commonly seen in infants <6 months of age. These infants are paradoxically at the HIGHEST risk for severe, life-threatening coronary artery aneurysms because incomplete presentation often delays life-saving IVIg treatment. Classic disease requires ≥4 of 5 mucocutaneous criteria.

questions.q: A 16-year-old girl presents with widespread hypopigmented patches exceeding 2 cm in diameter involving the trunk, arms, and neck. She does not have a primary facial involvement. Which variant of pityriasis alba does this presentation most likely represent?
opts: Classic pityriasis alba with facial predominance
Extensive (generalized) pityriasis alba with female preponderance in teenagers and young adults
Pigmenting pityriasis alba with blue-colored lesions
Follicular pityriasis alba confined to the pilar apparatus
questions.exp: The extensive variant of pityriasis alba is characterized by widespread lesions not limited to the face, with individual patches typically exceeding 2 cm in diameter. This variant predominantly affects teenagers and young adults with a distinct female preponderance, contrasting with classic PA which favors children and the facial region.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Teenage GIRL sits on a GIANT SPREADING MAP (trunk and limbs covered with LARGE PATCHES—bigger than 2cm rulers scattered across her body) while the FACE ROOM remains untouched.

questions.q: A 9-year-old girl with alopecia areata is found to have HLA-DRB1*0401 and HLA-DQB1*0301 haplotypes. Her mother has a history of alopecia totalis. Which genetic finding is most significant in predicting disease severity in this child?
opts: HLA-DRB1*0401 and HLA-DQB1*0301 are specific markers for severe, longstanding alopecia totalis or universalis
CTLA4 and IL-21 polymorphisms guarantee progression to alopecia universalis
The presence of these HLA markers means she will definitely develop alopecia totalis within 1 year
HLA-DQB1*03 is the only genetic marker associated with severe disease
questions.exp: HLA-DRB1*0401 (DR4) and HLA-DQB1*0301 (DQ7) are specific MHC Class II genetic markers for severe, longstanding alopecia totalis or universalis, in contrast to HLA-DQB1*03 (DQ3) which is a general susceptibility marker for all forms of AA. These markers increase risk but do not guarantee disease progression. The child has a 6% lifetime risk due to her mother's history, significantly higher than the general population's 1.7-2%.
questions.source: [paeds Day 28] Alopecia areata in children + JAKi
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: In the castle's HLA HALL, the DR4 and DQ7 ROYAL GUARDS are SEVERE enforcers—they mark the path to TOTAL castle destruction (totalis/universalis), while the common DQ3 guard lets ANY level of attack through.

questions.q: A newborn presents with an armor-like shell of yellow-brown hyperkeratotic plates separated by deep, diamond-shaped red fissures, along with ectropion, eclabium, and mitten-like hand deformities. What is the most likely genetic defect responsible for this classic presentation of Harlequin ichthyosis?
opts: Biallelic mutations in KDSR gene encoding 3-ketodihydrosphingosine reductase
Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in ABCA12 gene encoding an ATP-binding cassette lipid transporter
Monoallelic mutations in filaggrin gene affecting stratum corneum formation
X-linked mutations in NSDHL gene encoding cholesterol oxidase
questions.exp: Classic Harlequin ichthyosis is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations (usually nonsense or frameshift) in the ABCA12 gene in >93% of cases. ABCA12 encodes an ABC lipid transporter responsible for loading lamellar bodies with lipids and proteolytic enzymes; its failure prevents intercellular lipid bilayer formation in the stratum corneum. The pathognomonic clinical features—armor-like plates with diamond fissures, ectropion, eclabium, and mitten deformities—are characteristic of this severe barrier defect.
questions.memory_palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a medieval CASTLE ARMORY (ABCA12) filled with LIPID TREASURES in diamond-shaped crates. A broken ABC LOCK (loss-of-function mutations) prevents the lipids from reaching the castle WALLS (stratum corneum), leaving the HARLEQUIN JESTER frozen in his armor with red diamond cracks, ectropion eyes, and mitten hands—the jester's grotesque costume now a prison.

questions.q: A 3-year-old heterozygous female carrier of X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (XLHED) presents with patchy sweating abnormality over the trunk and limbs. Dermoscopy reveals alternating bands of sparse and normal-density hair in whorled distributions. What is the underlying cellular mechanism responsible for this mosaic phenotype?
opts: Random somatic mutations occurring post-natally in epidermal stem cells
X-chromosome inactivation (lyonization) creating two distinct cell populations with different EDA1 genotypes
Antibody-mediated destruction of sweat glands in specific dermatomes
Segmental overexpression of the normal EDA1 allele compensating for the mutant allele
questions.exp: Heterozygous female carriers of XLHED exhibit mosaicism due to random X-chromosome inactivation (lyonization), resulting in two populations of cells: some expressing the normal EDA1 allele and others expressing the mutant allele. This creates the characteristic alternating bands of normal and absent sweating following Blaschko's lines, along with whorled patterns of sparse hair distribution. The female carrier phenotype is therefore milder and patterned, in stark contrast to the severe generalized disease in affected males.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman is referred for evaluation of a sharply circumscribed, jet-black macule on her thigh measuring 6 mm. Dermoscopy shows a central dark structureless area with symmetrical radiating peripheral streaks. Which genetic alteration is most likely to drive this lesion, and how does its epidemiology differ from classic Spitz nevi?
opts: BRAF V600E mutation; occurs equally across all age groups with male predominance
Kinase fusions (ALK, ROS1, NTRK1); occurs primarily in children under 10 years with no gender predilection
Kinase fusions (ALK, ROS1, NTRK1) or HRAS mutations; occurs most commonly in the third decade with female predominance (2:1 ratio)
NRAS mutation with isolated chromosome 11p copy number increase; occurs mainly in adolescents aged 10–20 years
questions.exp: Pigmented spindle cell nevus (Reed nevus) is a variant of Spitz nevus that uniquely presents in the third decade of life with a strong 2:1 female predominance and favors the lower extremities, particularly the thighs. Approximately 55% of Spitz nevi overall are driven by kinase fusions (ALK, ROS1, NTRK1, NTRK3, BRAF, RET, MET), and another 15% by HRAS mutations. Unlike classic Spitz nevi which favor children and adolescents, Reed nevi present in young adults.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A 25-year-old QUEEN sits on her THIGH throne wearing a REED dress with a STARBURST crown—two LADIES flank her (2:1 female ratio), all spinning kinase FUSION pinwheels.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with poorly defined, round hypopigmented macules covered with fine white scale on his cheeks. The lesions fail to tan with sun exposure. Histologically, mild spongiosis with follicular plugging and atrophic sebaceous glands are noted. Which mechanism best explains the hypopigmentation in this condition?
opts: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes mediated by HLA-associated pathogenic antibodies
Eczematous dermatitis disrupting melanosome transfer from melanocytes to keratinocytes, potentially worsened by tyrosinase inhibition from dicarboxylic acids or low serum copper
Neoplastic transformation of the pilar apparatus leading to loss of pigment-producing cells
Immunobullous disease causing basal layer separation and pigment loss
questions.exp: Pityriasis alba is fundamentally a low-grade localized eczema and post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, not an autoimmune, immunobullous, or neoplastic disorder. The pathogenesis involves eczematous dermatitis disrupting melanosome transfer, with additional inhibition of tyrosinase by dicarboxylic acids from Malassezia or low serum copper.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a MELTING MELANIN FACTORY (melanosomes stuck in the ECZ corridor—eczema blocking the hallway) while TYROSINASE WORKERS sit idle, poisoned by sneaky COPPER-STEALING MALASSEZIA IMPS crawling through the castle.

questions.q: A 3-week-old infant presents with profuse, watery nasal discharge that has become purulent and blood-tinged. The mother's syphilis serology is positive. Which of the following best describes this clinical finding and its significance?
opts: Condylomata lata with secondary bacterial superinfection requiring broad-spectrum antibiotics
Syphilitic pemphigus with rupture of blisters leading to purulent discharge
Snuffles (syphilitic rhinitis)—often the first symptom of early congenital syphilis with highly infectious discharge teeming with spirochetes
Neonatal herpes simplex infection with syphilis co-infection requiring acyclovir and penicillin
questions.exp: Snuffles is the characteristic presentation of syphilitic rhinitis and is often the first symptom of early congenital syphilis, occurring in the first weeks of life. The discharge progresses from watery to purulent and blood-tinged, and is highly infectious because it teems with spirochetes. This clinical presentation in a newborn with positive maternal syphilis serology is pathognomonic for congenital syphilis.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A baby SNUFFLING like a pig at the castle entrance in week 3—his NOSE RUNS WITH SPIROCHETE RIVERS, the first herald of syphilis invasion in the royal nursery.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with clusters of small, discrete, flat-topped papules on his elbows and knees that appeared after summer holiday spent playing outdoors on grass and sand. The lesions are asymptomatic to mildly pruritic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Lichen planus
Frictional lichenoid eruption
Lichen nitidus with systemic sclerosis
Keratosis pilaris
questions.exp: Frictional lichenoid eruption characteristically presents as 1–2 mm discrete papules on elbows and knees following frictional trauma during warm months in children aged 4–12 years. The extensor surface distribution and seasonal/activity-triggered pattern are classic. Unlike true lichen planus, it lacks basal layer destruction and represents a friction-induced atopic variant.

questions.q: A 6-month-old male presents with recurrent unexplained fever (38.5–39.5°C), sparse lightly-pigmented scalp hair, and delayed eruption of teeth. Physical examination reveals frontal bossing, depressed nasal bridge, periorbital hyperpigmentation, and absent sweating on palms and soles. Skin biopsy from the palm shows total absence of eccrine sweat glands in the dermis. Which genetic mutation is most likely responsible for this clinical phenotype?
opts: Autosomal recessive mutation in the EDAR gene encoding the EDA receptor
X-linked recessive mutation in the EDA1 gene encoding Ectodysplasin-A ligand
Autosomal dominant mutation in the EDARADD gene encoding the intracellular adapter protein
Autoimmune-mediated destruction of sweat gland tissue with HLA-B27 association
questions.exp: X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (XLHED/Christ-Siemens-Touraine syndrome) accounts for ~80% of HED cases and results from EDA1 gene mutations on Xq12-q13.1. The clinical triad of severe hypohidrosis (causing infantile fever), hypotrichosis, and hypodontia with conical incisors, combined with characteristic facies (frontal bossing, saddle nose, periorbital hyperpigmentation) and absent eccrine glands on biopsy, is pathognomonic for XLHED in an affected male. HED is fundamentally a developmental ectodermal disorder with NO autoimmune pathogenesis.

questions.q: A pregnant woman with primary syphilis presents to antenatal clinic at 20 weeks gestation. She receives adequate penicillin treatment immediately. What is the expected outcome regarding fetal infection?
opts: Fetal infection will still occur in approximately 70-100% of cases despite treatment
Fetal infection will be almost always prevented, but stigmata will develop due to late treatment
Adequate maternal treatment before 16-18 weeks of pregnancy almost always prevents fetal infection and irreversible stigmata
The fetus will develop mild congenital syphilis manifestations only, as maternal immunity provides partial protection
questions.exp: Adequate maternal treatment with penicillin before the 16th to 18th week of pregnancy almost always prevents fetal infection and subsequent irreversible stigmata. Although this patient is treated at 20 weeks (beyond the critical window), the principle demonstrates that early treatment timing is crucial for prevention. The fetus achieves full immunocompetence by 18-20 weeks, before which inflammatory tissue destruction does not occur.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a PENICILLIN SHIELD blocking the CASTLE GATES before week 16-18—too late and the invaders (spirochetes) have already breached the royal nursery (fetus).

questions.q: A 9-month-old girl with roseola infantum is found to have small erythematous papules on her soft palate and uvula during examination. What is the eponymous name for this characteristic enanthem?
opts: Koplik spots
Nagayama spots
Pastia lines
Forchheimer spots
questions.exp: Nagayama spots are the characteristic enanthem of roseola infantum, consisting of erythematous papules on the soft palate and uvula. Ulcers on the uvula and palatoglossal junction are also highly characteristic findings of sixth disease. These oral findings may precede the appearance of the typical exanthem.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: NAGA (the serpent) YAMA (mountain) climbs the SOFT PALATE mountain in the mouth—tiny red papule peaks on the uvula throne room.
